local_scope: Skimmed content/foundations-and-the-fourth-amendment overview and node pages; did not read any s6-frontier-*claude* files. Every row was pre-checked by caption/party-name grep against content/cases/, _overhaul2/lake/_manifest.json, _run/s6-candidates/r7-queue-batch1.jsonl, and _run/s6-candidates/gated.jsonl.
inclusion_floor: page_candidate true only for missing controlling SCOTUS, binding-in-circuit omitted-question authority, or split-marker authority; narrower real finds are mention-only.
source_crosscheck: Page candidates were checked with non-CourtListener web sources: Justia plus LOC U.S. Reports PDFs for SCOTUS rows, and Justia full-text/PDF for the Tenth Circuit row.

caption: Burdeau v. McDowell
justification: Missing controlling state-action/private-search origin case for the Fourth Amendment Framework: the Fourth Amendment restrains governmental action, so incriminating papers stolen by private actors and later given to federal prosecutors were not suppressible absent government participation or knowledge in the taking.

caption: Ex parte Jackson
justification: Missing controlling early protected-papers/mail case for the Framework/Common Law Origins pages: sealed letters and packages in the mail are protected papers and may be opened only under a warrant satisfying the Fourth Amendment's oath, particularity, and seizure requirements.

caption: Marcus v. Search Warrant
justification: Missing controlling general-warrant/history application for Common Law Origins: mass seizure of allegedly obscene publications under warrants that let officers decide what to take lacked required safeguards and directly tied modern Fourth Amendment limits to the English general-warrant abuse lineage.

caption: United States v. Ackerman
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
justification: Missing binding-in-circuit digital private-search/state-action frontier case for the Framework's private-search doctrine: NCMEC qualified as a governmental entity or agent, and by opening an email and all attachments after AOL's hash report it exceeded any prior private search under Jacobsen/Walter.

caption: Roaden v. Kentucky
justification: Mention-only: real field-seizure application of Marcus/Stanford to warrantless seizure of a film, but narrower and better housed under warrant/expressive-material seizure doctrine; useful adverse reminder that expressive seizures get heightened Fourth Amendment reasonableness scrutiny, but not a foundations page candidate here.
